cases.title: Contention Wall
cases.description: Rust drives 100 OS threads through one shared AtomicI64. Kain currently has no user-level OS-thread fanout in LLVM, so this is the zero-lock collapse proxy over the same total increment count.
cases.fairness_note: Do not read this as a completed concurrency win. It is the benchmark shape Kain must graduate toward once collapse can be shared safely across spawned workers.

language_notes.javascript: Dependency-free Node uses a scalar proxy here so worker startup and SharedArrayBuffer scheduling do not dominate the case.
language_notes.python: Dependency-free CPython uses a scalar proxy here because locked threads would mostly measure GIL and lock scheduling overhead.

cases.title: Ghost Mirror
cases.description: Rust mirrors a 1 MiB payload through a std TCP loopback channel. Kain mirrors authority state with entangle and mutates a 1 MiB helper-owned buffer in-process.
cases.fairness_note: Kain entangle is currently in-process world mirroring, not a two-process transport. This case measures serialization/transport tax versus compiler-owned mirror semantics.

cases.title: Evolutionary Loop
cases.description: Rust uses runtime feature detection to choose a math lane. Kain expresses the same decision as converge/orchestrate lanes.
cases.fairness_note: Kain LLVM now carries multiple converge fast lanes and can route CPU-capability lanes through the native selector/cache. The lanes in this case are still scalar semantic proxies; it does not yet race AVX-512 kernels or persist warm autotune winners across runs.

cases.title: Scoped Ownership Memory Cell
cases.description: A smaller first-class ownership smoke benchmark: Kain uses collapse/observe/decay over a helper-owned heap cell; Rust uses an owned Box mutation and drop.
cases.fairness_note: This is a direct memory-lifecycle smoke, not a contention test.

cases.title: Branch Dispatch
cases.description: Integer match/branch dispatch with mixed arithmetic. This catches control-flow lowering, branch prediction, and basic optimizer quality.
cases.fairness_note: Both sides use deterministic scalar control flow and no external dependencies.

cases.title: Call Chain
cases.description: Deep small-function call graph inside a hot loop. This measures call overhead, inlining assumptions, and arithmetic lowering.
cases.fairness_note: Rust functions are marked inline(never) to keep this from becoming a pure optimizer-elimination benchmark.

cases.title: Memory Stream
cases.description: Sequential write/read over a helper-owned integer buffer. Kain uses raw memory helpers under collapse/observe; Rust uses a Vec<i64>.
cases.fairness_note: This is a direct memory-throughput smoke, not a SIMD memcpy benchmark.

cases.title: Allocation Churn
cases.description: Many small allocate/write/read/free cycles. Kain uses alloc_zeroed plus decay; Rust uses Box allocation and drop.
cases.fairness_note: This is intentionally allocator-heavy and will expose runtime bookkeeping overhead.

cases.title: Scalar Mix
cases.description: Hot scalar loop with top-level const expressions and a checksum guard. This case exercises LLVM top-level const resolution directly in the benchmark lane.
cases.fairness_note: Both sides use local top-level consts plus a deterministic checksum gate; this is the benchmarked path for the repaired const lowering.

cases.title: Recursive Sum
cases.description: Recursive integer aggregation in a hot loop. This catches call-stack lowering, recursion overhead, and tail-call assumptions without external dependencies.
cases.fairness_note: Both sides use the same pure recursive helper and identical loop counts; no runtime libraries beyond std builtins are involved.

cases.title: String Ops
cases.description: Repeated substring search and string length/indexing over fixed ASCII strings. This probes text lowering and branchy search loops without external dependencies.
cases.fairness_note: All languages use the same fixed ASCII strings and no dead modulo math; we intentionally keep substring search on the general path so the case measures string lowering rather than benchmark-specific specialization.

cases.title: Array Scan
cases.description: Nested array indexing and weighted accumulation over a fixed integer list. This stresses bounds handling, indexing, and simple loop lowering.
cases.fairness_note: Both sides use fixed local arrays and the same loop counts; there are no imported containers or external dependencies.

cases.title: Machine Stones Shatter Loop
cases.description: Hot field iteration over a fixed particle set. Kain authors a clean array of `shatter struct` particles and LLVM lowers proven loop indexes to cached SoA lane bases; Rust and C++ hand-author the equivalent SoA arrays.
cases.fairness_note: This isolates shatter memory-layout lowering rather than pulse or teleport. Kain's row uses compiler-owned shatter SoA lane bases; Rust/C++ use explicit structure-of-arrays source, while JavaScript/Python mirror the same field arrays without native layout control.

cases.title: Semantic Singularity
cases.description: Kain-only fused semantics pressure case: axiom/pulse/shatter/teleport feed world/entangle/patch/law state, converge/orchestrate transform it, modern microcell actors answer requests, and collapse/observe/decay guards the shared memory cell ring.
cases.fairness_note: This is intentionally Kain-only. It is not a cross-language fairness row; it is the integrated semantic pressure vessel for checking that Kain's weird memory, world, actor, and intent systems compose inside one native LLVM benchmark.

language_notes.kain: Uses ABI v3 actor ask/reply, native machine-stone runtime hooks, two entangled world fields, repeated patch/law/converge/orchestrate work, teleport handoffs, and raw shared-memory collapse/observe/decay in one checksum-guarded loop.

cases.title: Struct Method Dispatch
cases.description: Construct small records and call an instance method in a hot loop. This catches aggregate layout and method-call lowering.
cases.fairness_note: Both sides allocate records on the stack/logical value path rather than external heaps.

cases.title: Option/Result Tagged Values
cases.description: Hot loop over Option and Result creation, branching, and unwrap paths. This probes tagged runtime value overhead.
cases.fairness_note: Rust uses std Option/Result; Kain uses its native tagged runtime path.

cases.title: Async Ready Chain
cases.description: Hot loop over immediately-ready futures. Kain uses native async/await lowering; Rust uses a Tokio current-thread runtime and async fn await points.
cases.fairness_note: This intentionally measures ready-future async overhead, not IO wakeups or task fanout. Rust is built with Cargo because Tokio is an external runtime crate.

language_notes.rust: Cargo release build with tokio rt/macros; no C++/JS/Python lane for this dependency-focused comparison.

cases.title: TCP Loopback Tokio
cases.description: Repeated localhost TCP echo handshakes. Kain uses the native net substrate; Rust uses Tokio TCP with async accept/connect/read/write.
cases.fairness_note: This compares usable local networking paths, not identical schedulers. Kain's current native TCP facade is synchronous around readiness helpers; Rust's lane is Tokio async IO.

language_notes.rust: Cargo release build with tokio net/io-util/macros/rt; no C++/JS/Python lane for this async-runtime comparison.

cases.title: Rayon Parallel Reduce
cases.description: Large deterministic integer reduction. Rust uses Rayon parallel iterators; Kain currently runs the equivalent scalar reduction as the durable slot for future actor/parallel lowering.
cases.fairness_note: Do not read this as a completed parallel Kain comparison yet. This case exists to track the gap against Rayon until Kain LLVM exposes proven user-level data-parallel fanout.

language_notes.rust: Cargo release build with rayon; intentionally Kain/Rust-only per the parallel-runtime comparison.

cases.title: SIMD Lane Mix
cases.description: Integer dot product over twin buffers. Rust and C++ use explicit AVX2 lanes when available; Kain currently runs the same data shape through scalar LLVM memory helpers.
cases.fairness_note: Kain LLVM does not yet expose first-class SIMD intrinsics in the benchmark lane, so the Kain row is the scalar proxy against explicit AVX2 in Rust/C++.

cases.title: Native Map Lookup
cases.description: Repeated fixed-key hash map lookups over a small string-key table. This probes map dispatch, key hashing, and boxed value overhead.
cases.fairness_note: All three rows use small in-process hash maps with identical fixed keys and deterministic lookup schedules.

cases.title: Manual JSON Roundtrip
cases.description: Dependency-free manual parse plus serialization over two small JSON payload shapes. This measures parser/string work without hiding behind vendor libraries.
cases.fairness_note: This case intentionally stays manual and dependency-free across languages. In this checkout, Kain LLVM JSON builtins still fail to link, so the benchmark targets parser/serializer work rather than builtin-runtime availability.

language_notes.kain: The native LLVM lane currently reports unresolved externals for json_parse/json_object_new/json_object_set/json_string/json_get_*; this manual JSON path keeps the category benchmarkable while preserving that linker gap as telemetry.

cases.title: Filesystem Stream
cases.description: Repeated temp-file write, streaming copy, and readback over a generated text payload. This catches filesystem syscall overhead and runtime path glue.
cases.fairness_note: All rows generate the same payload, write it to temp storage, stream-copy it, and validate the copied text before cleanup.

cases.title: Process STDIO Loop
cases.description: Repeated child-process spawn plus stdout capture through the host shell. This measures command launch and stdio pipe overhead rather than computation.
cases.fairness_note: This is a Windows-first case over cmd.exe stdout capture. It is intentionally shell/process heavy and should be read as host-substrate overhead, not pure language throughput.

cases.title: HTTP Server Concurrency
cases.description: Local HTTP request handling over many short POST roundtrips. Rust uses Tokio tasks for concurrent client batches; Kain currently drives the same local route surface synchronously.
cases.fairness_note: This keeps the category visible while Kain's current native HTTP surface is still synchronous. Rust measures real local async concurrency; Kain measures the matching request/response semantics without async task fanout yet.

language_notes.kain: The current Kain row now completes repeated local POST rounds after the request-handle auto-release fix. Keep reading it as a synchronous semantic proxy rather than a finished async HTTP story.
language_notes.rust: Cargo release build with tokio net/io-util/macros/rt/sync; this is intentionally a Kain/Rust-only HTTP runtime comparison.

cases.title: Actor Ask/Reply Fanout
cases.description: Synchronous mailbox roundtrips fanned across four long-lived workers. Kain uses native LLVM actor ask/reply lowering over scheduler-owned microcell turns with synthetic reply-port refs; Erlang uses direct process mailbox request/reply.
cases.fairness_note: Both rows measure real request/reply mailbox roundtrips over four long-lived workers with the same deterministic checksum schedule. Kain now runs actor handlers as bounded nonblocking microcell turns, so blocked compatibility actors no longer consume the pooled scheduler lane used by the benchmarked ask/reply path.

language_notes.kain: The Kain row performs one unmeasured warmup ask per worker before timing. Native LLVM actors compile to KAIN_ACTOR_ENTRY_KIND_MICROCELL_TURN and poll mailboxes with kain_actor_try_receive under a default 64-message turn budget.
language_notes.erlang: The Erlang row mirrors the same one-shot per-worker warmup so both rows measure steady-state mailbox traffic instead of startup effects.

cases.title: Unicode String Heavy
cases.description: Repeated substring search over mixed UTF-8 payloads with multilingual text and emoji. This catches string traversal and byte/character handling under non-ASCII inputs.
cases.fairness_note: All rows stay on UTF-8 strings with the same payloads and manual substring search so the case measures real Unicode-heavy traversal rather than ASCII-only shortcuts.

cases.title: Allocator Large Object Churn
cases.description: Variable-size large-buffer allocation, touch, readback, and release in a hot loop. This exposes allocator cost and object-size sensitivity beyond the tiny alloc_churn case.
cases.fairness_note: This case deliberately varies buffer sizes and touches first/middle/last cells so it stresses large-object churn and fragmentation pressure instead of only tiny boxes.

cases.title: GPU Graphics Submit
cases.description: Low-level native graphics session, buffer, pipeline, draw-command, and present submission in a hot loop. This is the current Kain-owned GPU/graphics benchmark surface.
cases.fairness_note: This is intentionally Kain-only for now. The benchmark measures the current raw native graphics submission path; a comparable bare-metal Rust/C++ lane has not been added to this suite yet.

cases.title: FFI Shared Call Stress
cases.description: Repeated native shared-library calls through one tiny C ABI function. This is the direct FFI-call half of the missing callback/FFI category.
cases.fairness_note: This covers direct shared-library call overhead inside the normal suite. True closure-to-C callback trampolines are still not implemented in Kain LLVM in this checkout, so the callback half remains a known language gap and the dedicated `benchmark/ffi_boundary` lane stays the deeper ABI-tax probe.

language_notes.kain: This case uses a case-local `KAIN.toml` plus `use c::ffi_boundary_shared` and a runner-built shared library copied beside the executable at benchmark build time.
